Here im one to which Imlyard, the famous traveller, who smut over a great part of the world both civilised and uncivilised, gives the results of his oleervation, on women. "1 have observed, lie eays, " among all nations that the women ornament themselves more than the men that, wherever found, they are the earn< civil, kind, obliging, humane, tender beings ; that they are ever incl ined to be gay and cheerf ui, Conan us and modest. They do not hesitate, like men, hi perform an hospitable or generous ution, one are they haughty. nor arrogant, nor eupereilious, but toll of court., and fond of society, indus- trious and economical, ingenbitur; more Diable in general, to err than man, hut in general, alm more virtuous, and per- forming more good actione,then he. I never addreseed my- self in the language of decency and friendehip to a woman whether civilised or eavage, without receiving a decent and and friendly answer. " Among the fugitives in the rebel ranks was the resolute woman who, alike in the council end 011 the field, was the mul of the conspirators. Clad in the attire of a man, and mounted on hormbiek, the Rani of Jhansi might have been seen animating her troops through- out the day. IChen, inch by inch, tli. British troops passed through the PAWL and when reaching ita remold, Smith or- dered the Hussars to charge, the RAIIi of Jhansi boldly fronted the British horsemen. When her misrules failed her, her horse, in spite of her efforts, carriwl her along with the others With them elm might have esermd, but that her horse stumbled and fell. A hussar, ignorant of her sex and her rank, cut her door. She fell to nine no more. That , eight her devoted followers, determined that the English , should not tarot that they had captured her, even dead, • burned her holy. Thmi died the Rani of Jhansi. A case is related of a man who would not eat unless hi. food was stolen ; in consequence of which his at- tend iht humoured him by placing his food in a corner, where it 4ippeared hidden, but mold easily be—so to speak— purloined. A lady was also affected with this monomania so etrongly that upon her trial for theft eke stated that she had each a mad longing to possess herself of everything she now that if she were at church she could not refrain from stealing from the altar. Dr. Roth, the famous American physician, inform on that a woman who 1,19 exemplary in her obedience to the moral law except the Eight Command- ment was so addicted to larceny that, when she csuld take nothing more valuable, she would often at the table of 3 friend secretly fill her pocketa with bread. Lavater also states that a doctor of medicine coold not Isive his patients' rooms without taking something away unobwrved ; and his wife searched his pocket., and returned to their owners the kolvet, thimble, scissors, fie., which her husbusl ofo stracted. The wife of another physician had so streng a propensity to steal that on making purchases she endeav- oured to take something 3WAy that did not belong to her: and to,, German countesses appear to have been guilty of the sante vice. The almoner of a regiment of Prussian cuiramiers, a welbeducated man, frequently on parade stole the handkerchiefs of the officers ; and one unfortunate man was so far under, the influence of kleptomania that, being , nigh unto death, he actually secreted the snuffbox of his confessor.

• A YORKSHIRR SCNDAT SCHOOL AND ITI SURPRISING Resm.m.—The lower orders In Yorkshire,atys the "Editor's ' Drawer " of Harper'a Maga:ble, have not tlie reputation of being the politest nor yet the most amiable people on the face of the earth, and the following incident will be accepted by these who know Yorkshire, without a shadow of doubt or surprise. Some months ago two young undergraduates, , whine father had an estate not far from 'York which they had never sem, took a fancy to go down there for a part of !their vacation, and one of them, who expected eventually to ! go into the Church, thought he saw here a capital oppor- i tunity to practice bin elocutionary powers, and at the same time benelit his fellow-man by establishing a Sunday echool 'ln a large disused summer-house on the estate. So the peasantry from far and near were asked to assemble, and did assemble to a considerable number In the summer-houee on the first Sunday afternoon after the invitation Wei promul. gated. Their frehaviour, however, was anything but orderly or rempectful, and the embryo elemyman got an extremely unpleasant impression of Yorkehire inannere and piety before the lecture was over. Not despairing, however, he conlially asked all present to come again on the following Sunday which invitation, to judge by the tumultuous applause that followed, was aerepted by the entire congregation. During the week a happy thought occurred to him to give to his hearers instead of a dry addrms of the stereotyped kind, a Bible lecture illustrated by drawings ; his brother was A very good draught:imam, and alter tome persuasion consented to oaken eerie, of sketches in chalk von blackboanl, while the budding clergyman delivered a descriptive lecture. The subject chosen was the story of David and the Goliath ; a story full of draniatic power,which he thought would appeal strongly to his hearers ; and in this he was not mismken. The audience woe very large and at first unmannerly; but as the etory went on, accompanied by rapid chalk sketchee of the character, and costumes, the famous combat, Sr., the turbulent crowd quieted down and manifested the utmost attention and interest to the end, especially while the sling and Its construction were being described. The young reacher mturned home highly elated with his purees.; he assured his brother that they were sowing good need, and in time m abundant harvest would be reaped ; it was an um tilled but fertile soil, and he felt that there was great hope. Half an hour later a man came running to the Manor-bouse ion state of intense exci,ment: “Please,sirs,Maeter tiemge and Master Harry, ran you come and help to stop the riot In the village? All the men and boys hereabout are a stonin' of each other with slings, like them Master Harry thawed in the pictures to-day. There's nigh onto SO people in the fight, and there's hardly a whole pane o' glass or a whole skull left in the village !" •

How Too CIIINFSE COUNT Tnin.—Forty-five centuries ago this Oriental people had constructed astronomical in- ' etrumente analogous to the qu:idrant and armillery sphere, which enabled them to make olwervatione remarkable for their accuracy, and making poseible, even at that remote period, the formation of a useful calendar. Their present system As a very complicateel one, hut, like , arrange- went el this ingenious people, works with absolute accuracy once the principle of its procedure is understood. An in- , teresting account of it is given in an article on Chinme New IYear Customs, in the current Ilarprr'J Mrip,ine, under the title of 0 The Sixth Year of Qwung See." Like that of the Hindoos, the Chinese civil year is regulated by the noon, and from the tune of the Hon dynasty, two ceturim before Christ, hoe begun with the first day of that moon during the enuere of which the sun enters their sign of the zodiaccorre- sponding to our sign Pisces. They have also an astronomical year which i. color, and for the adjuntment of these solar and lunar ymrs, employ a system similar to our leap-ymr plan, except that instead id an intercalary day every fourth year, as in the Gregorian calendar, they in.. an intercolary month, occur ring alternately every third and second year in periods of nineteen. For inettnee, Into year had an inter- minty month ; the next one will come in 1882, again in 1884, then in 1887, etc.,—two intercalory months in lice years, or eeven Ic nineteen years. The year, therefore, con- tains thirteen or twelve montha according ,ts it lone or has not an intercalary one. A month has either twenty-nine or thirty days, the number of days being intended to corre- apond to the number of days which the moon takes to niake the revolution around the earth. A mnnth, bleed, means one moon, the earn. Chineee character being treed to indicate both. So, too, the number us.l to indicate the age of the moon at any time denotes also the day of the month ; thus there is Away, 0 full moon on the 15th, no moon on the Ist, etc. Consequently, the moon alway prments the name ap- pearance on the sane day in any month from year to year. This plan is particularly convenient for farmers and sailor% whose memory is thos materially assisted in remembering the changes of moon and tides. The era used by the Chinese in their historim is, next to that of the Jews, the oldest ern- [doped by any nation, as for on or four thousand years they hove for chronoldgical purposes made use of a aeries of daily, monthly, and yearly ,yeles of 60. New Z.LAND Fanwiwo.—At the Maidstone Farmers' Club last week, Mr. lialcombe, having been introduced y the Chairman, delivered a very interesting lecture on New Zealand, of which we can only give a brief extract, taking the following ea being probably the portion of g.sitest agri- cultural interest In getting in our crops, and in laying down our land in gr..s, we make use of machinery and labour-saving appliancen to the greatest pomible extent. Nothing hoe surprised me more than to find in England the absence of those appliancm we use in getting in our crops. den rule, we use double and treble furrow plough.. Our divisions are larger, to that we can go on for half o mile or no without a torn. It anyone in New Zealand used two men to a plough, we should think be was going to the bank- ruptcy court, and four or lye homes can be driven with very little trouble by only one man. The saving of traction in Liking off the great sole plate, and the gain by the use of double and treble furrows, is enormous. The cost of our horse keep is less than in England, and we have gross all through the vear. We hardly ever stable our horses, but for two months in the year we put • cloth over them. Then again we get in our crops with thence of as little manual labour as poesible. The crop grows and ripens, and we never have Input inc hoe to weed it. I have hanlly ever seen a poppy, whilst twitch is unknown. If land does get foul we lay it down in gram and graze it and the grass will soon clean it, SO that in two or three ymrn we can turn it up again. When the crop of wheat is ripe, the reaping anel binding machines are set to their work. and very soon do it. The climate allows us to thrash our corn in the field without stacking at all, or if we do stack it is very lightly stacked, and we do not trosalle to thatch it, but put the butt end of the sheoves the right Inan'. We have to pay a grml deal tor our labour, and our hinire ere shorter ; but I In say dis- tinctly,. a practical agriculturist, and ns 00000 who has employed labour for 26 years, that I believe from what I have eeen of English labour that we get our mones-'s worth out of our high-priced labour, more than you do out of your comparatively low-priced labour. Wlini IS T 131.1.1. 111:51,11/4011,—One hundred and fifty year, ago farms were being thrown on landlords' hands pretty much after the name fashion an at present, and there appeared to lien strong probability of the English tenant farming aim becoming extinct, Co boil were the times. Jethro Tull had a poor arable farm on his hands which he could not let, aid fortunately was it for posterity that such was the cam, an it led to his originating • syn.m of hus- bandry of an invaluable nature, and with it a new implement, front which our modern drille have been constructed. Tolls system was that of growing crops in double and treble rows, with intervals between the rows sufficiently wide for the hond-hoe to keep them clean, but also with broader inter- vals between the mei. of rows for admitting the plough and horse.hoe. When he wrote his lost account of bin elms., he had 120 acres of wheat thus planted, which had a promiaing appearance of yielding well, and Tell had for 12 years thus continued the samesysteni, and found it to pay much better than any other for wheat growing, although it woo pursued without the slightest manuring. In fact the idea on which Tull acted WIS. that tillage by attrition end aerifying in• duences, provides pabulum for plant nourishment just the some as the application of manure direct, and that hew,, in the right is sufficiently proved by the experiments of Ohs Rev.S. Smith, of I...isweedon, who, for over 30 years,carriel on the Tullion husbandry, growing heavy crops the entire period without the application of a single particle of manure —only the Loisweedon wile a more costly and impracticable method than the original Tuition, in.niuch as the wide in. tervals had to be dug by the spade. Other disciplen of Tull have found his system perfectly successful, by relying on the aid of horse tillage for the wide intervals; and .Cobbett, in 1823, furnished an instance of it Herefordshire farmer, who had grown wheat on the aline land, without manure, nix succeasive yearn, the crops of which averaged 23 bushels per acre for the entire period. nt9 the general necessity of sowing arable down to grace appears to be founded on the costliness and unprorit of practising alternate husbandry, would it not be worth while to make a more general trial of Tulle method of growing perpetually crops of grain, with- out manurial application, on the mine land, although on alternate sites—ae the entire virtue of the system connists in the interval being aeritied and furnished with elements of fertility by tillage while the cropped lines are producing. Landlords having poor class farms thrown on their hands often ask what they can do, except sow them down to gram. We reply, " Acquaint yourselvm with what Jethro Tull did ender similar, or even worst circuoistancm, and you will foul his method by far the more remunerative one of the

Erecrisic Hant.—At the Academy of Sciences, in Paris, a paper wan recently read by M. Arena, in which he recounts some experiments he made in the North of the Sahara. By passing a pocket comb through his hair or beard he ',re- duced sparks of 5 to 7 centimeres in length in hot, dry weather. Horses' Mile presented still more striking electrical phenomena, which he attributes to the ill-conducting horny matter of the hoof effecting better insulation front the earth than is obtained by the human foot. He states that the sparks above deseribol were obtained from himself without insulation, and that insulation increasee the ineneity ef such phenomena- I have made similar experiments myself, using different kinds of combs, and find that real tortoise- shell is much more effective than ordinary born comle, and horn better than bone ; also, that vulcanite is about equal to tortoiseshell and that—other conditions being equal— the experiments are more successful define frosty weather, with easterly winds, than at other times. This is, doubtless owing to greater drvness of the air. My experiments de not confirm what Ni. Arndt state-v respecting insulation, is insulation by the feet. I tried this many years ago, and, finding no perceptible difference, concluded that the neon,. earn insulation is effected by each individual hair on its own account. This was confirmed by the fact that dryness and length of hair appeared to le—next to atmospheric dry- ness—the chief condition of Puente. If I am right, the length of the hair on the horses tail has far more to do with electical excitability than the supposed insulating power of its hoofs. Cats are celebrated for their electrical properties, and they have no hoofs. Their far itself is highly electri- cal, gems know by experiments made upon their separated skins. A cat's skin, ova fox's tail, is an admirable rehear loran electrophorus. Some years ago I witnessed, in Edin- burgh, same very striking experiments made by an eminent tram(dienne On her own hair. By rapidly rubbing it in a dark room with • tortoiseshell comb, lit remeniber rightly) she brought out brilliant flashes, produced bra multitude of sparks, accompanied with loud crackling. Her hair was re- markably black, gloesy, and long, anti she had a theory of her own on the subject. She believed tbat the electrical propertiee depended upon excitability of temperament, or mt-like" intensity, as she termed it. My more prosaic theory, that it depended simply on the nou-conduction or insulating efficiency of long, dry, non-pomaded, glossy hair, was scornfully rejected. She told me that the electrical phenomena were far more brilliant in Canada, durit, the dry, interne frosts of that climate, than in Edinhur,!.. that fib.ree of eilk there clung to her fingers, and moved curiously about She spiders' t.--Gentlemen's alfeintrnee.

Under the Appellate Juridiction Act, passed in 1970, two lords of Appeal, were, for judicial purposes, eroded peers for life, that Act retaining in the House of Lords the Court of Ultimate ' Appeal, and the Act prescribing that that court should con. tint of the Lord Chancellor and two lords of appeal, the latter to be created pecrs for life. Innis Blackburn and Gordon were under the Act croatnd life peers. The House of Lords in February, 1858, successfully opposed a motion for the creation of life peerages. In that year a peerage for . life only, with the Saito( I,nlVVensleydale of Wvnalrydale, was granted to baron Sir John Parke. The House of Lords ! opposed his sitting and voting non peer for tife, and on July I 25, 1958, he was created a peer in the usual way, with the I tile of Lord Wensleydale of Walton. A hill for creating life peerages was rent a second time in the House of Lords on the 27th April, 1889, but afterwards their lonlships rejected it. Minnows, St. Helens.

div.p: Mt EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 11, 1880. THE WAR AGAINST RITUALISM. I THE ILLEGAL DISTRAINT AT

The firs. T. Pelham Dale wail brought up before the Judges nt dm Queen's Bench Division on Monday under a writ of habeas corp., and bitt counsel, Mr. Charles, Q moved for the rev. gentleman's dmacharge from imp icon. cent. Mr. Charlm enntendtd that tire process a contempt resorted to under the Public Worship Act could note this ease be legally applied. that the iseiVence of inhibition for disobt.dience was Ilnet, and that the requisition, the munition, and the inhibition were bad ku the face of thenk. Ile imin- .ined that time Judge had not complied with the requisite prelimirkarim to enable him to excrete flee office of official principal of the Arches Court of Canterbury, that the writ of contumacy wm bad and insufficient, and nine that the Act did not authorise imprisonment. The learned caumel bad not concluded his arguments when the Court rose. Mr. Dale WA. returned in custody to Holloway Gaol. The Rev. T. Pelham Dale writing to the Bishop of Lon- don's statement relating to his congregation wmplains that for yeare the mmt persistent elf°nt have been made to drive away him choir and congregation. He mune that his real proaecutore are the Church Amociation, and he tells the Bishop that he holds that the Zwinglian Calvanism which this Association seek, to force on him m the only allowable doctrine to be held in the Church of England is a heresy : contrary to Holy Scripture and the teaching of Christian antiquity. This being so, the controversy between himself and that Association is hopeless, and the appeal to law it. I mere means to enforce their views upon him and through himaelf on the Church at large Time Bishop of Rochester, in a letter to the churchwardens of St. Paul', Walworth, on the recent appointment to the living, Flays he acted in the belief that, his clkuice having been made, the parishioners would prefer an immediate an- nouncement from his own lips ton more tardy information judiciously distilled through the pen of a secretary. Ile thinks there need be no fmr either that the activities outside the Church will he diminished, or that slovenlineee or in. devoutness will become perceptible within, by the absence of illegal ceremonial. . . . . _ . . . .

The legal arguments in Mr. Dale's cam were continued re Tuesday in the Queen's Bench Division. Mr. Cherie, Q.C., concluded his Wars.e in eupport of the application for the discharge of Mr. Dale. 011 the same side Mr. Poland con- tended that Lint Pots.. had no jurisdiction under the statute unless he were patio motion by the Archbishop of Canterbury. Dr. Phillimore having been heard om the same side. the 'Attorney General semarked that in every case wttliout exception Lord Peng tnce hot simply obeyed the rules which he had been ordered to follow. Dr. Phillimore MI Wednesday concluded hie argument in the Dale case, and the Attorney General proceeded to show cause on behalf of Lord Pengince against the rule which , had been obtained, olwerving at the outset that he should be able to give a conclueiye answer to the objection. that had been taken ...hat the course which Lord Penance had follows'. Sir H. James contended that as Lord Pen- . stance held his apmiintment by express direction of the statute of 1874 he hail conformed to that which wee im- posed upon him by the Act, and that he then became by virtue of that statute official principal of the Court of Arches. He further contended that the failure to take the oath of eupremacy and make the declaration was immate- rial in thie cam. Fortnerly no one but an ecclesiastic could sit as judge in an ecclesiastical court, but that had been , altered, and as Lonl Penzance Waco layman the canons had no binding effect mmn him; he was not subject to the j ern. law. His lordship had been placed in his office by etatute, he eat by virtue of an Act of Parliament and he • 11.1 performs' every obligation which the Legislature had told him to fulfil. With reepsetto hi rules, 010 Attorney General sudmitted that what had beeo done throughout by Lord Penatece waa in exact accordance with the forma and regulations of the Public Worship Regulation Act, which , forms had the approval of noire. authorities than Earl Cairns I and the late Sir A. Cokl lon 00 the point raised ae to the form of the rerptisition, the Lord Chief Justice re- marked that there could be no doubt that it was made to the Judge, leaving tu him the liking of .y tinse and place within the centre of the requisition. 'rho Attorney General then arldremed himeelf to the objections to the monition and to the form in which it wan issued, and said Lord Pen- tane° would not desert the existing rules which governed Ids procwhire. During a discussion on the powers given under the Church Dicipline Act and the Public Worship Regulation Act, the Lord Chief Justice remarked that dim obedience to the low under any circumstances was a very grave thing, but it WAS seri"us matter to his inbred whether in emir rases av the present imprisonment was in- tended. The hearing was further adjourned. The Solicitor General addresaed the Court on Thursday In the Dale cam, subniitting that Lord Pensince had the powers which the statute law gave to such a Judge in an ecclesiastical cause to enforce the ordere of his Court, and that he had acted strictly in accordance with the statute. He argue 4 that there cleat Le some means of enforcing the order of inhibition which the Act ire .11 provided, and that it would be ridiculous if there were to be au inhibition which a man might set at nought, and the more an when was an inhibition to enforce obedience, upon which the Lord Chief Justice remarked that this form of resistance to authority was a new incident. The Solicitor-General re- peated his contention that it was essential to the due ml- mitristration of the low that whatever orders a court gave it should have the power of enforcing, anti in thie case im- prisonment TOLIS the means of enforcing obedience. Mr. QC, aditreses] the Court on behalf of the church- wardens, the promoters of the suit, contending that it wail a serious thing torn subject of the Queen to take it upon hinrself to my that an order of the Court was to trivial a thing, and that or so entirely disagreed with it that he did not think it worth while to regard it, and would not do so. Such disobedience would strike at the very root of civilised society. Mr. Jeune followed on the same side, and the further hearing wee adjourned. Mr. Dale has asked the Queen to use her Royal preroga- , five to right a grieve. wrong" was acknowledged cry General Ponsonby, who stated that the appeal must take tho ! form of a memorial. Upon the receipt of this littler R.. Dale again brought the case before Iler Majesty, appealing j to the Queen as a wife and .1 mother to take pity on her and her children, and asking wnat they must suffer when they saw Mr. Dale "a prisoner for conscience sake, driven to choose between us and what he most solemnly believes to be his duty to God." To thie memorial Mr. Liddell replivl that it has been referred by the Queen to the Secretary of State, and AP regrets that he is unable to adviee Her Majesty to interfere with the proems of law in the ease.

S_L. - RESUMrnON Or THE CASE. At the St Helens County Court, on WeinereLly afternoon la,A, beim e thy sitting judge, Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, the mats of Cordate v. Kirkham came OD again for hearing. It will be remembered that the plaiotiff, a foreman copper- amith. residing in Brook-street, claimed et the detente., who is an auctioneer, the 0r,., of LSO for darnagm for an illegal trespass on his property. At the last hearing the matter was adjourned, when the case for the pLiintift one laid before the jury.—Mr. Swift again appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Norden, of Liverpool, for Cle defendant The c,se lasted Dearly five hours, anti during the heariLe, the court was crowded to excess, and the Interest excited was shown by repeated applause when some good point was rained by the prosecuting or defending solicitor.. Mr. Norden, in addressing the jury for the defence, stated that he should not attempt to follow the example of hie friend (Mr. Swift) and use the language he indulged icon the last occasion, Mr. Swift dirt certainly take all the pos- sible heves. he ever heard an advocate take In the unmea- sured terms he applied to the defendant. He called the ' defendant ovoythiog vile end evil, and finished up by call- ing hint a rubber. He was sure that the expremiona that were used would ',eve no weight with the intelligent men he saw in the box before him, who had to try the case, not according to the amount of clap-trap oratory and decla- matory evidence but to actual facts. It was very easy to , indulge in epithetical remarks in a case of that kind, and I nothing in the world so took with people in court, and , nothing was SO calcubtted to exCite applause as oratory of that nature. On the one hand they had the female who went through a theatrical performance, and during the pro- cess of crying er the witneas box. alluded to unfortunate twine, and to the pathetic circamatance of defendant want- ing to take the cradle from underneath those interesting mortals as they reclined in the trooden structure prepared for their use. Those sort of things were advanced on pur., -se to get on the sympathetic side of the jury, but he . . . • . _ • "

pose to get on ton . , hoped they would take no notice of such. The remarks hie friend (Mr.fte ift) made to the jury he would never have demi to add,., to the judge, and he ta,k the liberty he had in villify;ng the defendant and holding him up to public, odium. Kirkham at the time of the distraint was doing a public duty. Ile was an auctioneer employed by the Cor- poration of St. Helens to compel the plaintiff to per, and discharge • public burden which lie like all othere had to bear. The plaintiff del not pay his rates, and the Corporation "natty resolved to make him, because if . everybody refused to pay, and were not made to do eo, how I were the public burdens to be supported. The plaintiff re- ' fused to pay his rates, was suntmuned on the 6th of August, and on the 9111 of August an order for payment w. made. Up to the With of August he 11.1 not paid anything, end no a warrant of distress was issued, and the defendant was en. tooted with the executem of that warrant. He W.la cot/I- ntended to levy the sum of £2 145. 6d. and the cost, of keeping the distr., and he would show them by the evi- dence that the distrene was levied in a fair manner, and not in the way the plaintiff's solicitor said it wag at the last I hearing. Upon the eubject of illegal charge., there was no doubt that all eherges should be conformable to the sche- dule kid down in the Act of Geo. 111. But in that case the defendant was not bound by those charge, at all, berause the warrant stated that he had to levy the distress, and charge reasonable expenses for so doing. IHis Honour 'I Isere is nothing :dated in the warrant which overrides the Act of Parliament. Mr. Norden : I think the term . reasonable charge, " in toed in cone vtion with distresses for rent above £2O. 1 eubmit as a matter of law that if it had been intended by the warrant to hare meant merely what is given in the Act it would have said no. Hie lionnur The form of warrant ie applicable to any 'amount of money levied, but then the charges are limited. Do you deny he has charged more than the statute allows him? Mr. Norden said he could show that the charges the de- ' fendam had made were in consequence of a epecial agree- meet with the plaintiff. When the defendant entered upin poeseseinn it wa, hie duty to remove the goods at once, but. I instead of doing so, upon the plea of the plaintiff he allowed them to remain until such time as the plaintiff could find money to pay him, and pot • man in possession, to whom he paid ss. a day, being 2s. 6.1. in excoee of the usual cherge. His Honour said that the etatute allowed the defendant 2s. 11,1. per dey, and if he made an agreement with the plaintiff for 5e., he (defendant) had no right to take the money out of the produce of the sale. He had <barged £5 4s: 10,1., being an exc. of £2 0,. Sel and the jury only could give hien the fair value of the goods less the rates. I Mr. Norden said the defendant had receiver] 15e. from the I plaintiff for that special charge, and an account of it had I been rendered. His Honour: He has herecharged 25e, for a Tall in pore leaden five days. Ile cannot charge more than 123. 6d. Mr. ?ionlen: Not although there woo an agreement. His Honour No: not if he agree, to give him £lOO. Mr. Norden , Well, your Honour, 1 must take your ruling, , and without further deley I will call my witnesses. ' Mr. Sefton, one of the collectors for the borough, was called, and esid that the plaintiff wee, in Auguet last, in arrear with hie rates. Witness applied not less than three times for the money. The witness put in the warrant he received to take onto distr., on the plaintiff's premise., sigaed by E. Johnson," justice of the peace for the county of Lincaster. . Mr. Swift objected to the warrant, as tl:ey had no evidence that Mr. Johnson eigned it. Mr Norden' He ira magistrate and Mayor of the borough. Mr. Swift He is not. I say he is neither the Mayor nor the horse. (laughter in court.) His Honour Will you show us the authority for the Mayor signing such a warrant? Mr. Norden The Mayor is es-ofeio magistrate for the borough. His Hoeour Yes, but not for the nounty. He signs himself here an a magistrate for the county of Lancaster. Mr. Swift Yea and he ie nothing of the sort. There are gentlemen ready to bite their finger nails off to be made county magistrate,. Mr. Norden ) Well, if he signed himself "Ambassador Ex- traordinary to the Court of Pekin" it would not vitiate the stentrionti. His Honour: I say it would. Mr. Norden: Well, he is in effect Mayoral thebmough. His Honour: But be did not sign it as Mayor. Mr. Norden) I will prove that he was acting as borough Manor. Him Honour' It seems to me discreditable that a man who is acting in an official capacity should sign his name is something that he haa so business. Mr. Swift It assumes that the Vi arrant was leaned by a competent person. (To the Judge). Had oil we better get on with the witness? We should have been half way now. eft Haden Yee, we should have been but for your in- terruption,. (To witness)' this not Mr. Johoson Mayor at the thne he signed this warrant? Mr. Swift I object to that question. Mr. Norden: You object to anything. We had better mete yon Mayor. Mr. Swift Well, I am going on that way for it. (Laughter.) Ilia Honour Let to get on and have iota nonsense. The witness was then crose-munined by Mr. Swift with each vehetnence that his Honour aeked [tint to moderate his language. He elicited from the witness that he waa not in the habit of .soiling hie kick" by dietraining a per- son'. goods, and that in such casm he appointed persons to do it. Williani Kirkham, the defendant in the ease, said he was an actioneer, and was employed in August last by the last , witness to execute a warrant on the plaintiff's goods. The last witness told him he was to levy £2 14e. In pursuance of that warrant he went and put a man in pos- eeselon. He told the plaintiff's wife that he had come to distrain for £2 143. for water rates, ss. 62. for his costa, and 17s. Id. to save the plaintiff being summoned on another rate. Plaintiff's wife said she had not got the, money, and witness thereupon left a man in poseession of , the premises. promising to see her husband before removing , the goods. Mitnees called again and RAW the complainant, and he seemed excited on hearing what he had come for, muttering that he did not know where to get the money. , Plaintiff afterwards said he Woe not a tenant of the house, but merely managing it for the landlord, Mr. Wilcock, and I that the landlord ought to pay the rates Witness saw Mr. Wilcock. and he refused to pay the talon, so he told the plaintiff he slmuld have to remove the goods at once, but plaintiff did net want him to du so. Witness told hint the law ooly allowed hint to charge certain ken, and that he c.mld not leave et man in possession at 25. 6d. a day; but ultimately it wasagreed, on the suggestion of plaintiff, that se. he paid to witne,e to allow a man to stay on the premises instead of removing the goods to him auction rooms. On the following Monday he .11,1 upon the plaintiff, and asked him if he had get the move, but he said he bad not. Wa- ne. then roil," Well, the sale will hive to take place to. morrow,"and plaintiff replied that it weuld have to done. On Tueelay morning following he vent to the plaintiff's house and taw Mrs. Coders, who steted that she had keen unable to get the money, and that witness could sell the goode, or "do what he liked with them." yide then appointed the tale to take place at two o'cloek, 'rand sent the bellman round in the usual way to announce the sale. He paid 311 s. to the man who held possession, and if he had removed the goals to his own sale-room he should have been able to pocket more money. Al the pale the brokers only bought about £2 worth of goods, and he never beard any complaint respecting the way in which the cab was conducted. The evidence produced at the last enquiry was absolutely false, as also W. the evidence saying that -he (witness) attempted to sell the cradle in which two children were dying. In many cases the articles fetched more than they were worth —for inetance, a man paid ss. for bedsteads that a fortnight after only realised 4s. Witneer did his best to fetch the higheee prices, and gave the plaintiff all the balance that accrued from the sale. Mr. Swift You ate an auctioneer, I suppose? Witnese: Yes. Mr. Swift It does not require a man of highly moral character to be an auctioneer, eh ? Witness: It requires ability. and I flatter myeelf I have it. Mr. Swift: Yon have contradicted ev,ey witness that appeared at the last inquiry. Wham: I believe I have done. Mr-Swift It is not the first time you have been en your trial. Witness: I do not see that tint has any, to do with .he cane. Mr. Swift In 1875 were you not convicted for travelling without a ticket on the railway Witness: Yes, and fined le. Mr. Swift In the following year you were fined for

anew+, Yen, my wife and I had a little bother. Mr. Swift: In the following year, 1878, were you not put on your trial at the assizes and convicted by a jury of your own countrymen, and sentence to two months imprison- ment for assisting to pull down a Loose over the head of a family ? Witneos hives not proved that I did it, but that I was connected with the conspiracy. Mr. Swift How many times were you convicted in 1878? Witness, None that I know of. Mr. Swift : Were you not fined for assaulting your wife ? Witness : Tes, / wee tined Is., and you, Mr. Swift, de- fended me.
• Mr Swift : And that is the reason why you gnt off so sassily? Witness : Perhaps so. (Laughter.) M. Swift Thew were y.O not tined 40s. the market by.e-laws ?

The maladies of the body politic are of too maligeaat a type to be further negleeted, sad already the air in filled with rumour, and orianier rumours of the romediea politioal doctors inland to apply to tkr• national cove,. The greatest giossk of the hour I. the diecontent in Ireland. The Government, it is well knipern, have occtipiori the reads in framing a lame for adjusting the land laws of that ealtappy country. The Cabinet have all elmtg been. guided in their ruin of the Sister Isle by the reflection that the disaffection now rampant oan only be adeetively removed by the eubstitution justenactenenia for the oppressive end one-eided laws which now opt.. to the great disadvantage of the tenants of time.. Not only the 4overnment, but the Hones of Commons iteelf, pledged to amend the law governing land tenancies in Ireland, fed last )sei Yr. Shaw Lefevre succeeded in extorting from the people's representatives a resolution oonisheil in them terms " In view of the expediency of a consider.. increase of the number of owners of land in Ireland among the oleos of per.ee cultivating it. sod, legielatien ehould be adopted for the purpose of increasing the facilities offered by the Mato with this object, and of securing to the tenants tbeopportusity of purohsee, ou 1.110 tele of property, consistently 'nth the ioterests of the owners thereof." The House thoo imeds committed tOthie pledge, and the Government hays already evinced

disposition to submit legislative proposids, based upon the broadest grounds of freedom and equality. The Irish Compensation Disturbance Bill was a measure that would have brought in its train greatsatisfsetion to the discontented people of Bris ; and the hereditary peers, seeing the iil blood their high-handed policy has evoked, no doubt now regret their swam.; rejection of that me.nre. At all events, the, enoere- moniooo mode in which they threw out that Bill has paved the way is a coming me.ure of far greater scope and importance. Whilst we have so sympalki with the .wets of eedition among the Irish people, nor the faintest wish to ast the part of apologists for the lantles..a which has been only too active lin their unfortunate coantry, we cannot bet ;Itmognise, in the reckless disregard of life exhibited in resisting the operation of the law of eviction, a die- content which no amount of coercion can utterly suppress, unless it be backed by resolve on the part of the authoritioa to abrogate the statute shioh places a tenant at the mere mercy of his landlord. Co.er- vatives would meet the wriee for redreee of griev.oes by. rerert to those old weapons, the stspension of the Ilab.e Corp. Act, and the intsrlitetion of martial pule ; but the application in the past of w.pons like theee has not .oe.ded in cr.hing that f.ling f wrong which has sunk NO deeply into the I.arts of ,he Idol, People. The attempts to rule Ireland with an iron hand have failed hitherto, just . they will fail in the future. No amount of coercion can induce a people struggling for freedom to forget or ignore the fraud, coed peenhitions t,f centuries, nor that relation between landlordism and tenant right which meats to the great bulk of the people penury and death. The ltiv of eviction tittle &cite lele hoe been too tali

• festering sore but it is doomed. In the words of Mr. Gladstone 'eviction is a sentence of death:" and the present Premier of England, when once he sets his hand to the plough, is not the man to check his paec until he has completely uprooted such a I deadly 'I opus tree" as that new blighting and de. I moralising ono of the fairest gems among England's , possessions. The conditions of tenancy are but little lose satis• factory in England and Scotland than in Ireland, and • thorough reformation of the land laws affecting the thrre kingdoma id only a question of gine. Numerous farms in England and Scotland are now tenantless, agriculturists refusing to be bound down by rigorous restrictions, and to be subject to dismissal from their holdings at a few months' notice. The law of eviction in Ireland is summary in its operation: and it iv not to be wondered nt that the Lich people should have bgorne tired of its exigence, when Eng • fish farmers are to be found demanding greater security of tenure, freedom of cultivation, and the I abolition of the law of distress for rent, and I Scotch farmers are 1-lemouring for the repeal of the law of " hypotbec." Why rent should be more sacred than any other debt surpasses our comprehension: and whys landlord should be in a position to tumble • defaulting tenant into the highway, after the latter has trebled or quadrupled the value of his holding, without compensation for unexlmusted im- provements., and at a moment's notice, would puzzle the very gods to divine. What our legislators have to remember in that the land WII/i created, and that it existn, for the benefit of the whole people, and not merely for the comfort and convenience of a forlunate few and that there should be no barrier to the Li nd being made to produce the greatest amount of benefit to the people. The land ought to be an easily and as cheaply transferred I

The Health Committee ' tutdoubtedly reward the Doctor's epistle or damaging to their reputation, and as one that , con not be gainsaid. Our member of the committee, however, ventured to hint that the Doctor " had greatly overdrawn his subject," but this remark in- ' stoutly led to other members admitting the truth and justice of the Dodoes allegations, one observing, and I another supporting the statement, that a tow days previously, when near the rvilway station, " he felt a sensation like biing shot at with a thousand pi., both on the face and hands." An attempt to transfer Dr. Ricketts' complaint to the Medi.' Officer of Health and to the Surveyor, for them to inquire into and report them., was met with an obseryation from the Medical Offieor that "he could only report what he had been saying for seven years. Hitt evidence was , given year M. year in his annual report, and he could only repeat what he had said before." This is sufficient corroboration of the statements made by Dr. Ricketts; and the Health Committee, fioding no other way out of the difficulty, instructed the Borough Surveyor to see to the law being put in force against the excessive emission of smoke and gas from chin:v. neys, and directed that the attention of Mr. Fletcher, the Government Inspector, should be drawn to the great prevalence of noxious vapours. If the Health Committee only put them.lves to the trouble of seeing that their instructions are duly carried out and the law enforced, Dr. Ricketts will have the satisfac- tion of finding that his labour has not been in vain, and the public will have the gratification of being permitted to breathe a purer atmosphere.

We are undoubtedly OD the eV() of a great change, and the wisdom of our hereditary legislators, whore folly in resisting the popular demands of the people has ou more than one occasion raised the queetion of the need and utility of an Upper Chamber, will again be put to the test. Mr. Moldiunies, the member for Warrington, who is a far•seeing politician of extensive experience, and who doee not lend himself to random utterances, took, we think, in his speech to the Southport Liberals, last week, a most wise and comprehensive new of the probabilities of the political future. Satisfied that the pres int lend laws in Ireland are indefensible, he pointedly demonstrated that the farming industry of England would receive considerable impetus, which would tend to the advantage of both tenants and owners, if long leases and freedom of cultivation were conceded to the farmers. No stronger dlustra• Mon of the wisdom of landlords surrendering these rendition* could ho furnished than the story he gore of an estate, on which long leases and freedom of cultivation are given, having, within a few years, been so much improved as to raise the rent roll from £1,400 to fis,ooo, and of a tenant, who 1118 left to ' farm at will, increm,ing in twelve years the value of hia worldly posimmions from .C 550 to £52,000. The hon, gentleman apprehends that the passage of a Land Bill will be a rough and knotty one. That the Bill will be suceessfully e:trried by the Government through the House of Commons ;he does not seem to entertain the slightest doubtof ; but when the measure reaches the Upper House the peers, he is of opinion, will reject it, as they did the Irish Disturbance Corn-, pulsation Bill. The measure will again go, he thinks, ! from the Commons to the Lords, who will repeat their ! treatment of it in the first instance. It is tube: hoped, however, that their lordahips will by that time have realised that they can no morn resist the popular demandsof the people than Mrs. Malaprop modem the advancing tide with her proverbial mop, and that, rather than raise about their ears a hornet's nest in ' the form of a renewal of the cry for the abolition of the hereditary chamber, they will bow to the ioevitable. But should they prove stubborn and persist in throw- ing out the Laud Bill in preference to yielding a single privilege of landlordism, it is not unlikely that the Government, after securing an extension of the suffrage in the counties, will appeal to the country, and leave their lordships to the judgment of the electors.

The essayist, Mr Page, who had for his subject " Electricity as taught in the Bible "gave a brief outline of the science of electricity and endeavoured to deduce those facts from Scripture by quoting various passages which he assertst were intended to bear en the sub- ject. Fancy relatienship existing between o the elegantly-bound kid-glored novel and a lump of fat bacon; between the dapprslooking individaal who handed Itheme packet of tinted note paper, with the blandest smile, and the Manly and often greasy cmtnterman who I dabbed into the child's basin some butter hot yet there , was • relationship. Bacon and books were both connected with the Anglo-Saxon weed " box "—a bench tree. Pigs • were fed on box nuts, and thin tablele of the bark were o used for covering books. To this day they spoke of booke being "in hoards." A reader was • "box-reasler," a pub- lisher • " box.er," and componition was "bon craft." I Tbm bacon and books originated in the aarne tree. Grocers 'Ol4 treacle, a word which had three meanings— via., • poimn for vipers, a cure for their bites, and mmething for youngsters to bite. As to draper& and their goods A lady purchased muslin, the name of which was derived from IMesopotamia damask, from the far-famed city of Damas- cus, ulics from Calcutta end ermine came from the Dominion rat. The word tailor came from "miller," focal. This trader wail willing to cut their cloth to any pattern, and rarely omitted to mit himself plenty of " cabbage." It was usual to stipulate with much a one to cut for a certain price. This word come from " a straw given in ' token that • bargain was finished. A man put on bis new suit, and the tailor told him he looked quite rtspectahle, which meant one who would bear looking at. This put the man into "exatacies ".t the transformation—that we., made to stand out of one's self. Alas for human joy, the clothe, . lumbago, did not wear very well and the man called the tailor a humbug. which meant mtnething very had, but how hod toner woe able to say. Mr. Robinson next spoke of words relating to home. The word spinster arose from the Anglo-Samna making a law that • woman Mould not be married until she had spun enough for her first household. Bachelor meant s lower order of knight ; and he had little doubt that the bachelor crept into the boom under the pretence of &misting to turn the spinning wheel, and 'violet there persuaded her to change her name. As to bridegroom. Verstegan said that on the marriage day he waited at the table and served the brirle, and so was her "groom," for the time being. Then follower' that which be need not fully dericrilx, as tome of them had painful re- membrances of it. It was two o'clock on a cold winter's morning, and Mould the father be very rdemy, and the baby very lively, he might possibly cry out in parental rasa 'Oh, bother the brat." This was • specimen of the de- terioration of mrd, for brat was formerly connected with politeness. 01,1 Gamoigne raid. 0 WS.. 0 ho,usebold !I the Lord. p Ataluisn's brats,

ol,l4;;:d.brood.—love the Lord Indeed." When a spinster became a wife her name was changed, but not her word, for wife was from "nehen," to weave. Husband meant house band the stay of the house. The word lady was from the Anglo Saxon lmfdian, • eerver of hread. The derivations of many Chritian names were next [mewl : then followed those relating to character, such an scoundrel. idiot, and black- guards. Next, words of feeling and words of parting Farewell was Anglo-Saxon. and meant may you have a good journey. Thin expressive formula was fast dying out torn vulgar " take gore of yourself." " A-dieu was a word conMiniug • p f simplicity and beauty, vie., "to God I commend you:" a most suitable expression for Christian paaple. %%des of thanks wore passed to the !adorer and the 6114, man, after which the proceedings terminated.

div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

I A monthly and special meeting of the Town Connell was held on Tuesday evening in the Council Chanthor, at the Town Hall. Pmsent : The Mayor !Alderman Pickruere) in the chair; Aldermen Webster, Kean, Davies, Harrison, Holmes, Chandley, and Burgess ; Councillors Fairclough, Greening, Wallington, Barker, Brown, Platt, Dixon, Per- cival, Woollen, Taylor, Woods, Broadbent, Monks, Sutton. Whittle, Ashton, Prancomb, W. J. Burgess, Jeans, E. Ureenall, junr., MAne,, Cresfield, Litton, and Ridgway; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), Chas. Chorley (borough treasurer), T. I.ngdin (borough surveyor), and J. H. Unman (medical officer). There was a good attendmice of ratepayers. On the motion of the Manor the minutes of the previous meeting were pmeed.

Alderman Hcarows mo;e7.l7lZat the sa`ary of Mr. Jobe Ileukinnon Gomall, the medical autwriotendent ,d dm In- , fectious Ihseases Hospital, be' ine-eased to the sum of £lOO per atom."' He said Mr. Gornall was doing a very large amount of work. If the members would refer to the mitiutes of the Sanitary Committee, they would tied that Mr. Gornall bed had in the hospital during tbe preeent vea,, from the let of January to the 30th November, 84 cases. He presumed it would he quite within the conceptimt of every member of the Council that a mediml treutlem.m at- tending to 81 patients suffering from diemsesof the character that came to the Infectious Diseases thermal, had a good deal of work to do. But that was not all the work that per- tUn to the dutiee of the medical officer connected with the hospital. He had the charge of the nurses. 11 a mime had to he removed, or did remove, the inedic.d officer had to look out for and find another to take her plum. Ile bed to take the entire charge of the whole institution. It could not ho exmcled that the members of the Sanitary Committee mild be going down to the hospital day by day to look after it ; and he (Alderman Burgess) might as well at once eay that the good managerneutuf the hospital depended entirely, or ahnost entirely, on the management of the surgeon who wan placed in charge of it. Mr. tiornall had been mediml °dicer to that institution for, he suppo.,l, some twelve: month. or a little more at a salary uf £5O a year. The Sanitary Committee knew and felt at the time the appoint- ment wee made that the eatery was only a temporary our. It could not be supposed fora moment that the salary a gentleman who bad had a large sum nmorrovrpootopoo his education wm to remain at that amount. 't he Sanitary Committee never dreamt of such a thing. But the committee I hod had the opportunity very recently of combining in oriel officer the appointment of medical oflimr of health, the surgeon on the hospital, and analyst for the borough. By the combination of these officef they had moored a gen- tleman who would not have any private practice, bat would devote lie energies to the dim:harge of the duties of those office% together with the appointment of medical officer to the Rural Sanitary Authority and vaccinator to the Board of Guardians. With the exception of thme two appoint. mente the whole of the time of the nit...lima officer would be at the disposal of the Council or be devoted In the diseliarge of the duties per Mining to the appointments connected with the Council. Ito member thought £OlO was to,o much for the services of. gentleman who attendml to the hospital and LAW toot everything was going on in a proper. and satisfac- tory manner, he hardly envied him of his feeling. Councillor MONKS seconded the motion. Councillor WHITTn., said he was of opinion, when a ques- tion of this kind was • uhmitted to the Council, the tolled ! information should he given to all points. Mr. liornall had only held .11111 01 his ‘dfices about six weeks, and yet this was the second application for an incresee of rotary, and they did not know but what they might have another at the cleat meeting. Alderman Biogess had informed hint that it tem intended to raise Mr. Go, ILO I's salary for all his public appointments to at least £450 A year, end eid not see why the Council could not he treated witb similar con- fidence. Mr..Gernall war receiving as medical officer of health £lOO, or borough analyst £25. now .F. 50 or mmtiml superiatendent of the Infectious Dis.ses Hospital £5O, which it was proposed now to raise to £100; as public
.--/i73.1;;07t117-We have nothing to th, with thaf. Ahlernyto Iknov.ss: I want to know what we have to In with the public vaccinator. The Mayon: Mr. Whittle hoeo sat down.

.... Alderman BLIMESS: low not going to reply to that. Councillor DIXON mid it was his intention to oppose the motion on the ground that! he thought If the increase of the salary was granted to Mr. liornall it would be simply to insult some of their friends. fie conntlered the way he hod treated Mr. Waring, better known to some of thorn as Mr. Fell, was very painful indeed. Alderman Burgess saki he hail to do a very large amount of work ; lad, if the medical officer was to continue to done he had done to Mr. Waring's child, there was no doubt the work would increaco very much indeed. As Dr. Fox had said—and he (Cone- cube Dixon) thought they had a right to take another medical officer's opinion as well as Mr. liornall's—tbeechilil need not be removed from its home to the hospital— ! The Maxon: 1 think you had better confine yourself to ! the question. ! Councillor DIXON said on that account he could not vote to give an increase of salary to Mr. Gornalk for if he was to continue to interfere with people who provided proper !accommodation, as Mr. Waring did, the work would be very great and, in addition to that—, • "

The MAl'ort You are going beyond the question. Countillor NEON woe very sorry for that, because be thought it was one Of those eases which ought to be very well ventilated in the Council, at they were giving that night, or were asked to give, a reward to the man who had done that to some of their personal friends. The Mayon: You must not argue on this point. It isnot C question to be discussed. Councillor Duo, I say if the doctor is to treat every person's children in the way ho has done this, the work will Decrease. ,

Tho Moron- Yes, you can broadly state that. Councillor Coosrlit. did not agree with Councillor 1/ixon's argument. He believed Mr. blornall was a con- scientious nmn, and would only recommend cases to go to the hospital that he believed absolutely necessary. It did not follow that two medical men would agree in opinion. It was a very old saying that doctors sou:Oboes ‘liffered and it was quite possible that there might be a difference ol But Le did soy this for Mr. tiornall. that he knew faun one medical man in the town that he had shown great courtesy : and great consideration to the medical gentlemen in the ' town, and he (Councillor Crostield, was very pleased to hear it, because he thought it teal ye, desirable that their ' medical officer should he on good terms with the medical men of the town, The proposed salary of £lOO year was filed not time ago, and it woo only to conform to the orders of the Council that the motion had one up that night. Its was sure if any geutleman would consider the matter im- partially he would not think £lOO a year was an excessive salary for the work that had to be done. It, did not think it Wail fair for Councillor Whittle to bring in the other items he had mentioned, because they had nothing whatever to do with it. It was just a question of whether Mr. Gornall was entitled to £lOO a year for the work he would have to do in connection with that hospital, and he thought Mr. Gomel' was richly entitled to it.

The Ex.llevon asked if Mr. Gomall we going to give the whole of Ms time to this and the other appointments of the Corporation, it did not eay se in the minutes? Alderman BUBO., It has already been motel in this Council Chamber that on the appointment of If,. (Somali as medical officer of hmlth, as successor to Dr. Joseph, be uave up all private practice and devoted himself entirely to the public duties that pertain to the borough. and the appointmenta that he hold, under the Board of Guardians— , the one being medical officer of health for the rural district and the other public vaccntator..

- Alderman Ilanntsow said he thought if the Council were to appoint an officer in connection with the Infectious Hospital they would hardly expect to give one only £loo. Mr. Gorvoll had the reputation of being a duly qualified medical practitioner, and for anything he had heard to the contrary he alwaya undersloal Mr. Gomall a. a capable, alcient, and courteous gentleman. Of course he could not shut his eyes to what !le had seen in the paper during the last week in reference to Mr. Waring's child. That he did not think ougbt to be considered on tn. occasion. If Mr. Gornall, in the exercise of the duty entrusted to hint, bad acted in an arbitraly Inanner, and if his judgment was founded on the wrung side, it was clearly the duty of the Sanitary Committee to take the only step they could take to remedy that evil, and it was not necesxtry for him at all to describe what that process might be. Whatever Mr. Gornall had done in reference to Mr. Waring must stand its own bottom, as the saying was. It wat a separate and distinct thing for which he would be hereafter held respon- sible. Ile should feel it bin duly to support the resolution. Alderman KEAN did not think the members of the Coun- cil would like to give leas than £loo.

ICouncillor PIit;;CIVAL supporied the committee, as he r thought it wag matter of justice. If there was an under. standing between Mr. Gornall and the committee such as had hoen described, he thought it only right it should be carried Oct.

! BrilOOSS, in reply, said he thought the subject was exhausted. .11ear, hear.) It was only necessiry for Min to sty in reply to Councillor Whittle that the Council had nothing whatever to do with the appointments that Mr. diornall might bold unddr the Board of Guardians, or in connection with the Board of ituardians. All he had stated was that Mr. Hornell, in his combined capacity of medical officer a heelth,suigeon to the Infectious Diseases Hospital, and zie public analyst, would be paid by the Corporation, subject to that motion being adopted, £250 a year. But why Councillor Whittle insisted. as a member of the Sani- tary Committee, to talk about £.150 a year was beyond hie cninprehension. He knew nothing of what Councillor Whittle was speaking about, and did not care to know. Councillor IVntxxte U Ills correct.

Alderman Itcnoms said he knew it was correct that Mr. Gornuil, for his combined offices, wua in receipt of £450 • year. He know it very well ; and why should not he be I' Was Councillor Whittle a man who supposed that an educated man, a man who ha I had expended up...n his edu- cation as a professional man an amount of money that was often expended and must be expended on such men, was to be tabooed because, by the sacrifice of his private practice. and in the anibition—tiecause he was glad to say it was the ambition of Mr. Gornall—that he could render a public ser- vice in the discharge of a public duty, was prepared to take the combined offices for £2so—a thing they could not get done by the lowest menial in the profeasion be far as Mr. Waring 's chit Ism concerned they must per nit him to say that that was not the place for him to give an expla- nation of that subject. There were reasons and very good and sufficient reamina why the Council should not speak of it. He was told ion public newspaper that announced this matter that a public enquiry was to be .nede in the matter. He hoped it would be. He could only say that so far as the cane referred to by Councillor Dixon and Alderman Harri- son was concern.' there was no member of the Sanitary Committee who had anything to do with it. It did not per- tain to them. It was not their work, and they had had nothing whatever to do with It. If Councillor Dixon named the matter. pertaining to the Sanitary Committee he was labouring under a delusion. If the gentlemen—not Mr Waring—who had brought the matter prominently before the public would, ea they said, cause an enquiry to be made in the matter no one woold be more delighted then himself. to trusted they would hare a public enquiry, and that the truth would preeail, and the right would come out of it. (Hear, boar.)
On the motion being put there were loud criee of Aye and •No.' but the Mayor thought the. Ayes " had it. The Metort Do. any gentleman wish to divide the Council o.n it!
: There is no doubt about it. The MAYOR I think myself the Ayes have it. The 'notion eras then parsed.

The committee having considered the letter of Mr. Sutton, dated 901.1, October, together with the charges made by the Warrington Corporation, amounting to £l5 ss, it was ordered that the clerk communicate with Mr. Sutton stating that the cont. mittee had reason to doubt their liability, and they also con- sidered the charges exorbitant, and had decided to rtfer the seine for the Board's conskleration and Law Clerk's opinion. —The necessity fur hospital eccommaittion for the district was again discussed, and it was resolved that the clerk cont. municate with the Ilaydock Local Board to swertain if they were willing to join the Commissioners in providing • small hospibtl which could be used conjointly for both townships.—Plans for additions to New Market Inn for Mr. Win. Melling, Rho for additional store-room and bakehouse, in Lord-street, for Mr. William Austin were submitted and approved. Mr. PENNINGTON moved, and Mr. FAIECLOCON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Hinter called attention to the bad state of the foot- loth along the Mains as far as Mr. John Ball, farmer, had control over it. In weather like the present it was almost impassable, but where the Railway Co. took it in hand it was kept decently. This end of Park road, as far as the archway under the railway, was also in a dreadful state. A IIiSCIIBBIIOI followed as to who was really liable to. the re- pair of a mire of the road, whether the Board, the railway company, Mr. Leigh, or Mr. Ball. Ultimately it was do-' cided to ascertain by writing to the railway company. 'The LAW Cm., referring to the letter from the clerk to the Warrington 13oard of Guardians, said there could be no doubt whatever that at the time the children were removed to the hospital, they were properly in the charge of the Warrington Union, being properly prdered there. There- fore the order for their removal to the Infectious Diseases Hospital coming from the Guardians, and the children being at the time in the proper custody of the Guardian, under a proper authority which was granted at Newton, the Com- missioners had no liability. The liability was upon the Guardians, and not upon the Commissioners. Mr. WINSTANLET thought Mr. Worsley's case was not as straight as he seemed to imagine. In the first place appli- cation was made to either one or two Guardians who hap- pened to be sitting there, but the proceedings of that coin- mitiee were not adopted until they were read before the Warrington Board and confirmed. On the Illth September, between two and three in the after- noon, the plaintiff was walking from Weston (which was a village about two miles frotn Runcorn), on the right band side of ths road, when he was driven into by a cart, the driver of which wati the defendant'. .errant. The old rum wae knocked down and very much shaken and .bruised. In il,litott on Torts it was held that a person driving a car- riage was not bound to keep on the regular side of the road. but, if not, be must use more care and keep a better look out than if he were on the proper side. A foot paseenger was not obliged ha keep on the pavement, and if upon the road it was not enough that • person driving a conveyance or carriage should give him warning to get nut of the way, to exonerate himself from carelessness. 'there was no continuooe parapet on the road in question in tide cam, and none at the point where the accident took place. He should be able to prove that the plaintiff was on the right side of the road, and on the side where the parapet would have been had one existed. The amount of damages claimed was very moderate, being only £2O. He should also prove that the old man would have been able to make that amount per year simply hy commission on his rents The improbability of Ids being Able to attend to his business again, and the expensea incident to his Hinesa would probibly be taken into account. Plaintiff's daughters had had todeave their work io order to attend to their father timing Ins bickness. —His Honour: But the expel:lees of the daughters will not he recoverable. They may he entitled to charge mmething for earring—Mr. lake said the evidence of carlesaness on the part of the driver would be shown by evidence to the effect that be was on the right eide of the road, but between the place where plaintiff was walking to the kerbstone on the opposite side of the way, was mine seven yards, show- ing that them was ample room for the driver to pass.—The plaintiff WAS then called, and corrolsnated this statement. It was found nearly impossible, on the part of Mr. Swift, of St. Helens (who appeared for the &fence), to cross-exantine kiln, on account of his extreme dodoes/I. M, William Garnett, dock and pier toaster, Runcorn, said he was at the house of Mr. Frodsham, near the scene of the accident, on the day when it occurred. He described hear-I ing the trap come -down the road at 3 rattling pace, and , then observing that it came to a stoppage very sudilenty, and lae going out to see what was amis.. He saw that the plaintiff had been knocked down, and he and the driver were both trembling. He asked the man how it wan he had run over the plaintiff, on which lie said, "Sure, I thought I ' would clear Tabu. and I called out to him." He next re- I marked." You ought to have .lopped you were not Kiwi- fled in running him down because he could not bear you." "Sure," the driver said, "if a thing coald be done twice, it would be done well." (laughter.) He then helped the old man into the trap and asked the man to drive him home.— Cross-examined : hoes he not look as well as ever he did ? No; he dues hot.—Now, d,,es not the plaintiff look very ! well? Yes, considering what he has suffered .—I know he does not look as fat and flourishing as you do? (Laughter.) Na; but we shall both, perhaps, look. bad Ache does when we are as old. (Renewed laughter.)—Mrs. Elimbeth Ann I Kenwright, widow, Western-road, Runcorn, also gave evi- -1 dace as to going to the place where the accident occurred itnniediately aftcr it took pIICO. The old man's hack was dirty, and he complained of having been under the wheels of the convey:tem.—ln cross-exanunation, the witness mid she believed it was true that the plaintiff mitered from an 1 aCCident about eleven years. Eight days after the mei- ; dent she saw the plaintiff going to church, and he mid he • was a little better, "but his hack was had."—Dr. Robinson mid he attended the phiintiff immediately after the acc!lellt, and he complained of his back. He appeared to be suffering , from the effects of a shake, and there was 3 slight die- • golouration of the lower part of his back not Lug* than a shil ling.—Cron-examined Ito you remember the plaintiff's I claim from a company once? Were you one of his I doctors then? Yes.-1 suppose that waa a good job for you ? No; I don't know that it Was ; and ; emtaidet your insinuation in lthWarrantable One—He got I WO, 'oelieve, and that would straighten him up, and tel would stand up like a man after receiving that ? (No anewer.)—Perhaps you have not over-dosed him with phy- sic? Mn. lan, not in the habit of doing that.—Perhaps you are Hoinmpathic, and helieve innmall doses? !re, tarn not. I —Arthur Riley, provision dealer, and son of the plaintiff, ' gave evidence esti° the various items front which hie father. , realised his living.—Mr. Swift mid that before making :toy remark. on the rase, he should prefer to call the driver.— , Thot.s Traynor, an Irishman, the driver of the sharolry, • mid that at the time of the accident he was driving at the , rate of about seven miles an hour. When about forty yards from the plaintiff, Ire called to him. There was plenty of, rootn to pass him, on the near side, without any <hanger. The old man appeared to get frightened, and he (witnme) pulled up on the spot. Ile Oct ontolthe converance, think- ing that the plaimiff Won drank or in a tit. Ile asked plaintiff where he lived, and he slid in Higher Runcorn, lie ' enquired if (witness) could give hint a ride. He agreed tn do an, and when he had taken hint about two or three yards from the place, where he found him. the mare moved. He I , ran to stop her, and when going back to the old man Intake I him to the shandry. Mr. Oarnett, and Sirs. Kendright came up. In reply to Mr. Garnett's queetions, he said lie hail not , run over the man. Ile then drove off with the plaintiff in , the shandry, and on the w.ty to Runcorn he asked Imo if there Was anything the matter with I him and he said "No but he was frightmed."—

Mr. Swift &Ala this waft one of those unfortunate cases for lan employer, where, however careful he might be in the I mlection of a servant, or however careful that servant might have been in the past, yet if he Amid be guilty of negligence the master was made answerable. Pereonally Mr. Johnann. , was not to blame in the slightest degree. tiecausi nobody could suppose that in selecting the man Traynor he chose other than one who he considered a competent And respom sible servant. 'file net question for His Honor to coosider I was whether Traynor was upon the occaalon of the accident guilty of any negligence by which the plaintiff suffered ' wrong :—that was to my, whether he did anything which a reasonable man would not have done. Mr. Swift then referred to the circumstances of the case in detail, and went ; on to say tkat the Judge would also have to consider whether any injury was sustained by the man's negligence. Ile contended that the plaintiff was himself contributory to any I injury which resulted to him. Mr. lake having replied, the Jmlge said that. considering the sufferings which the plaintiff had had to ! endure from the shock to his syntem, consequent upon the accident, he thought he was entitled to more than nominal damages, but not to much as Sr. He should give • verdict for the plaintiff of £5 and costs.

The lecturer, in the entree of his address, illustrated in totter manner the forms of I Christian work adapted to the voung, and urged that if the principle were carried oat of giving young people something to do—of getting them to work rather than working for thorn ; —it would be valuable as an agency in retaining the scholars, and bringing them into connection with the church. A col- lection was made, which amounted to £3 7s. 31. which, after defraying expenses, will be applied in aid of the school fund. The usual vote of thanks to the chairman brought the pro.dings to a close.
